title: Gypsum Overlook: A sliver of southern New Mexico history from 9,000 years ago - NewsBreak
text:
By Nicole Sanders No media credit provided. ,
1 hours ago
NEW MEXICO (KRQE) — Paleontologists are buzzing over new discoveries among the dunes of White Sands – from ancient tools, to old fire-pits, and even evidence of man-made structures.
Now, a newly-published study of their findings is shedding light on some of the earliest known New Mexicans.
Story continues below
They call it Gypsum Overlook, a site that archeologists say captures a sliver of southern New Mexico history 9,000 years ago. “The environment is changing from cooler and wetter to more of what we see today. Drier. More pronounced monsoons. It transitioned from grassland into the desert scrub that we see today,” said Holloman Air Force Base Cultural Resource Manager Matthew Cuba. “Pleistocene era… think of mega-fauna, mastodon, mammoth, that type of thing… That period’s ended and we’re now in the early Holocene, which is typified by drier conditions.”
Cuba discovered black structures and stains made by fire and the chemistry of white sands’ gypsum, which melts into hardened structures. The black spots show where fire pits were used by humans over long periods of time. “Dark black features against a stark white background, it was screaming at you from 15 meters away,” said Cuba.
But that’s not all they found – archeologists also identified the burned outlines of other structures. “Whereas the structures were these short term, one-time events. The structures burned, creating a thin rind of anhydrite,” said Cuba.
400 artifacts were found on site – something that’s rare of the time period. “It suggests they were harvesting something,” Cuba said. “But we were never able to get a positive identification of that. Just because it’s such a harsh environment out there.”
“Gypsum Overlook” has the oldest known evidence of structures in the whole region. But with dunes continually shifting daily, archeologists are always on the lookout. “I’m always hopeful that I’ll get a call from someone and say hey, we’ve got another one,” said Cuba.
In the areas surrounding the Tularosa Basin, the next oldest evidence of structures is at the Keystone dam site near El Paso. Those artifacts came about 4,000 years after this new site at White Sands.
